Every startup needs a 3D printer.


We got one for the Listen Labs office for the AGI hackathon. Then the team started building things with it for fun.

Shalin has printed a doorstop and kudos tokens for the team.

At our Hawaii hackathon, Hugo, Krish and Ole connected it to our CRM. Every time a rep closes a deal, it prints that customer’s logo for them.

Someone even printed a model of Florian’s head.

But my favorite is Listen Instant.

A few months ago, we started bringing a chef into the office to cook lunch and dinner for the team. Every day, Lisa our office manager, sent out a poll in Slack to ask how the food was.

Almost nobody answered. People had opinions on meals, but most of the team was too busy to stop and submit a review.

So one evening Hugo and Maddie decided to change that.

They designed and 3D-printed a small box with face buttons (from 😀 to 😞) and put it on the lunch table. After eating, people hit a button on their way out.

It takes one second, and now the lunch ratings come in every day.

This is one of the many things I love about the team at Listen. People here notice something that could work better and, instead of waiting for permission, they just go fix it.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
A good lesson in AI is that you need to check back in on the latest with every 3 to 6 months to try something that wasn’t possible before and see if it works again.

At no point in AI’s history is that more true than today. Just the past six months of model progress around computer and tool use, less context rot, better reasoning, multimodality, and deeper domain expertise in a number of key fields, these models are vastly more capable on what they can execute.

This is opening up a new vector of what AI systems will be able to autonomously work on. Essentially, anything with an API (and even many things without), we can anticipate that an agent will be able to control and utilize as an underlying capability to complete a process.

This means that we are no longer dependent on *just* the models generating everything from whole cloth, but instead they can fully utilize existing systems (or new ones purpose built for them) very effectively. This creates immense leverage for agents.

Security agents can leverage existing data feeds and cyber tooling, IT agents that can execute workflows reliably across software stacks, data agents that can migrate data or processes between systems, architect and design agents can leverage CAD and design tools, and on and on. And any of today’s tools that don’t work will likely be replaced by agent-friendly or OSS tooling that does the same. 

When you combine this with the domain understanding being trained into agents, you started to get autonomous collaborators for every job function and industry. This will open up a ton of new opportunities in AI if you build with this understanding in mind.

This sounds extreme and I wouldn’t have believed it even a year ago, but we’re starting to see plenty of examples of productivity gains that are an order of magnitude or two above output levels pre-AI.   

With the right harness, a deep understanding of your domain of what you want to build, likely a relatively new codebase (with some exceptions), a fluency of how to work with multiple agents at once, and a setup that makes it so you can test and deploy with limited friction, outputs on this level feel realistic in coding.    

What’s crazy is this gap doesn’t appear to be diminishing over time. You’d think that we’d see a convergence in the lines because of AI, but it turns out the more depth you had before -and willingness now to take a different approach- gives you crazy leverage. And that is only compounding as the models can take on larger work and harder problems.  

Right now this is most pronounced in software engineering for the obvious reasons. But there’s no reason we don’t start to see this in a number of other computer-use-sensitive domains like other scientific fields, AEC, finance, cyber, and more. Going to get quite wild.

Yesterday at BoxWorks, we shared a preview of Box Architect, a breakthrough new way to autonomously drive enterprise content management and workflows. 

Most enterprise workflows that deal with enterprise content today can be slow, manual, and clunky. Contract management and reviews, client onboarding processes, digital asset management approvals, vendor onboarding, clinical trial workflows, and thousands of other processes that span every industry. For the past year we've been building agentic capabilities to help automate many of the steps in these processes to bring the power of AI to streamline these workflows.

This is Box Architect. With Box Architect, enterprises get the full power of frontier AI to autonomously build, test, optimize, and run their workflows and manage their content. Box Architect effectively acts as an agentic operator of Box's core content and workflow capabilities -- like Box Apps, Automate, Forms, Doc Gen, Agents, core content management, and more -- to help customers design any content workflow in Box. This could be anything from building out a contract management system to helping optimize a data extraction pipeline by delivering higher accuracy results at lower costs by running a multitude of tests for you.

Think of Box Architect like having the world's smartest expert in enterprise content management, workflows, and data governance --including any industry domain-- right at your fingertips. And because frontier AI models are getting to near-superhuman levels of intelligence, they increasingly can help us reimagine workflows leveraging their depth of knowledge in legal, manufacturing, finance, healthcare, life sciences, and more. We no longer have to just apply automation to how things are already done, but we can use AI as a partner to think through the most optimal way to streamline our work.

posts.author: Alex Palmer
posts.text:
I went to an OpenAI Codex builder day with the goal of building a GTM agent swarm last week. Very normal sales-leader behaviour.

The job I wanted help with: finding companies worth a closer look & understanding enough about them to have a useful conversation.

Once you start building, you have to explain what 'worth a closer look' actually means.

A pricing page mentioning enterprise. A new hire in your target persona. A founder presenting at an event coming up. The more specific, the better.

Useful things to know but each still leaves a question.

For the research workspace, we kept the observation, source & possible commercial relevance separate. You can see what was found before deciding what to do with it.

Selling at Vanta, I might want to understand whether a founder is preparing for bigger customer's security requirements. A job ad alone won't answer for that. You need multiple signals, firmographic data & intent signal scoring all combined to get the right targets.

The output I want is something like: here's the change, here's the why it might matter, here's what we still need to ask.

That last bit is where the sales experience earns its keep. Knowing which question would actually change your view of the account.

Don't get caught in the messy middle - keep it simple & focus on relevance + action - as perfectly illustrated by brendan's meme.

Folk building AI into their GTM work: what have you had to explain to the agent that you previously just did in your head?

Big thanks to Ricardo Schmidt & Regina Lin for helping me out with the building infrastructure, memory setup & more.

Evals evals evals 

GTM evals are much harder than evals for code since there's no deterministic backpressure from unit tests (way to verify) but once you get one locked in (rubric based, examples of what good looks like and why) and figure out where you need them in a given workflow it is extremely powerful. 

There's two types based on feedback loop length: 

what we think good looks like right now, based on what we know right now.  Feedback is still human in the loop instant, but it is still not the full picture. 

The full picture is what the market says, which takes far longer to Brendan's point. You can try to gather more intent data/feedback to accelerate but ultimately you are still bottlenecked by reality itself. 

I think companies are going to have to learn what evals they need and basically encode their judgment and learnings into to them to get AI that writes copy they'd actually send/ads that actually convert/whatever and it is not going to be something widely "solvable" you're gonna guard your evals like they guard gold in Fort Knox since that is your edge.

Muse Spark is now a tracked model in Profound, alongside the Answer Engines you already track, like ChatGPT and Gemini.

It’s one of the models behind Muse, Meta's personal agent. However, tracking it is not the same as tracking Muse, and our research shows why.

When Allison Huang gave Muse Spark a memory file like the one Muse keeps for each user, 54% of its searches included details about that person.

Its shortlists got shorter too, from 6.5 products per answer to 4.5, which leaves fewer spots for any one brand.

On top of that memory, Muse browses merchant sites and searches Meta’s product catalog, which the model alone doesn’t do. That means a brand that shows up well on Muse Spark may not be the one Muse recommends to a particular shopper.

The model still shapes how Muse reasons about products. Tracking it shows what Muse Spark knows about your brand and helps catch incorrect claims before they carry into products built on it.

With Personas, you can also see how its answers change for different buyer types.

Nice work on the integration, Meera Parat and Federico M. !

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
There's a huge opportunity right now in being the deployment layer for AI into the economy. The amount of work it takes to change out workflows in enterprises tends to be far greater than anyone realizes or would prefer. Clearly this is what the applied layer of AI is going to look like in the form of software and agents, but also it opens up new services firms opportunities.

Legacy systems need to be moved to the cloud, data organization and access needs to be updated, software needs to be connected to agents in new ways, workflows need to be reengineered for agents, HITL needs to be figured out for the process, evals need to be generated and maintained, and the entire system needs to be continually updated as new models get released and new capabilities emerge. And the full list may even be longer.

AI is not the same as just deploying software. Software you generally did the implementation of an existing, well understood category of technology, then stepped back and the customer kept running. With AI agents, you're delivering actual work augmentation to the organization, which has a completely different set of complexities associated with it. You're no longer deploying tools that the company is merely enabled by, you're deploying work output in a process. Completely different implementation and enablement process.

As a result, this is going to open up lots of new kinds of firms and plays for existing firms to diffuse AI into organizations. We're going to see approaches by industry, by size of company, and by problem inside of companies. Traditional SIs will modernize and adapt (some will clearly not adapt as well), and new entrants will also be founded in this period that take advantage of this window. Great time to be an FDE or FDE firm.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

It took 2 years of getting ghosted and a wedding but in July, we finally did it.

I wanted the domain from the start and I first messaged the owner in February 2024. Unsurprisingly, he said no.

He had good reasons to keep it. He’d owned the domain since the late 90s, when he ran a drum and bass and jazz improv record label called Listen Labs. He also had 20 years of email and logins tied to it.

I kept trying anyway. Over the next two weeks I sent him at least 10 more texts. I offered to trade him listen-labs.com, and to write access to his old email into the contract. Bryan Schreier at Sequoia emailed him. I asked Sequoia to get Ev Williams to reach out too.

He said no again, but he was kind about it. He told me his journey with the domain wasn’t over yet.

For almost two years after that, I texted him every few months. At one point I offered to give the domain back if Listen ever shut down. Later I put equity on the table and I sent him a custom invite to our Midsummer party too. He didn’t reply.

Then last year I found out he had officiated a wedding for one of my friends, Jonathan Swanson. Jonathan reintroduced us, and this time, I was no longer just a stranger chasing his domain… He finally agreed to sell!

Two years of persistence for a domain. Completely worth it.
P.S. me getting ghosted for 18 months 👇

posts.author: Alfred Wahlforss
posts.text:
Today, we’re launching Listen Twins, 1:1 digital twins of your audience.

Some decisions move too fast for a full research study, like which ad cut goes live Friday, which subject line goes out Tuesday, or whether a promo leads with free shipping or 20% off.

So the call gets made on the best evidence available, often a year-old study, one champion customer’s opinion or a Slack thread.

Listen Twins bring customers’ voices into those everyday decisions.

A few things to know about twins:

1. Each twin is modeled on one real person. We interview them in depth and build their twin from that interview. If you twin 200 CMOs, you hear from 200 different CMOs, with their own budgets, teams and priorities.

2. Twins are trained on your specific use case, so product roadmap twins are different from marketing copy twins, and you can see exactly what yours were trained on.

3. You get 100+ answers in seconds, each with its reasoning and a confidence score. You can ask any twin to explain itself and trace answers and justifications back to the real person behind it.

4. When a twin doesn’t have enough information, it says “I don’t know” (shocking, I know)!

5. Every new study, piece of context and set of customer data makes the twins more accurate.

At Listen Labs, we use them every day. Eric and Jin interviewed a group of researchers about ad copy from 10 research platforms, then twinned them.
 
When we were deciding whether our billboards should lead with quality and trust or with cost and speed, 80% of the twins chose quality and trust. Jin’s team now checks with them daily.

Of course, as a human insights company, we’ll keep advocating for talking to your customers when time and budget allow. Twins fill the gap for everyday decisions where they don’t.

Excited to see what teams build when customer input can be part of every decision.

There's a lot of doom and gloom about AI right now.  

When I think about whether an industry survives it, I ask one question: why does this industry exist in the first place, and will that reason still be here after AI?

For law, the answer is simple.  Law exists to help people agree.  

Every contract, negotiation, and dispute comes down to people with different interests finding terms they can live with.  AI will change how that work gets done, maybe dramatically. It won't change the fact that people need to agree, and I don't see that fundamental need as a society going anywhere.

posts.author: Aaron Levie

What an insane day in AI. Both Anthropic and OpenAI have released updated models at the frontier. This would be big enough news, but the bigger headline for anyone building agents is that the models just became substantially cheaper, with the Opus 5.5 price cuts, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna dropping token prices by 50%.

The rate at which the cost per task (on a like-for-like basis) drops in AI is unlike any other type of technology in history. And every time the cost of AI drops, the use-cases you can deploy agents against dramatically increase. This is Jevons paradox applied to agents.

These improvements will directly lead to broader diffusion of AI in the economy as we can use agents to process all of our data, scan our code for security issues, read through all log data to make decisions, have agent swarms in workflows, and much more. The cost of tokens is directly correlated to these use-cases being opened up at scale.

It’s an incredible time to be building or deploying agents right now in the enterprise.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
There’s a massive chasm between the power of AI models and the ultimate workflows that enterprises are trying to automate. This gap is the opportunity for the applied AI layer to fill.

You need to connect the intelligence to workflows, often reengineer processes, aggregate the right context and data, allow for the right human in the loop experiences, drive change management, do domain specific evals, manage the security and governance of the data and process, and much more.

We’re going to see this layer emerge in every vertical and horizontal category. Platforms like Cognition, Cursor, and Factory for coding; Salesforce, Sierra and Decagon for customer service; ServiceNow Console and Serval for IT automation; Harvey and Legora for legal workflows; Box for document automation; and so on. 

And ironically, even as models improve at incredible rates, this layer still must exist - and may become even more important and useful. Greater capability enables even more complex tasks to be tackled, amplifying the challenges if you don’t do this well.

Was super fun chatting with Sonya Huang on all the things going into AI diffusion on Training Data podcast. Full podcast here: https://lnkd.in/gwKUkg3z

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. 

Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before.

What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before.

If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems.

Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
You're going to start hearing a lot about agent swarms going forward. This was the technique recently popularized by OpenAI, when they had an estimated 10,000 concurrent AI agents work together on breakthrough math problems. 

Here’s why this is a going to be a very big deal in the enterprise: we can finally make compute a critical variable in a large number of important tasks in the economy which wasn’t possible before.  

There’s a large amount of work in the world that is essentially only constrained by the amount of time that we put into research, data processing, discovery work, running tests, and more. All of this work is bottlenecked by our ability to plan, execute, review, and coordinate everything happening in these workflows. Which means we basically do very little of them today relative to their economic value.   

Agent swarms are the first real ability to parallelize this work in a way where - in theory - the only parameter that matters is how much compute you throw at the problem. Cyber security, life sciences or material science research, trading, QA testing, data processing, and many other fields are essentially compute constrained problems in the limit once models are good enough at these tasks.  

The breakthrough is that in a world where agents can use tools, write code, process data, have strong domain depth, and can coordinate with each other, you can begin to solve arbitrarily complex problems by setting the right goals and applying enough tokens to the problem. This changes a lot of fields as well as even the competitive dynamics in these fields.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
This is correct. The vast majority of enterprise workflows have not actually had agents applied to them in any meaningful way. The economy probably has this deployed < 1% right now.

At best you have a few automated systems in a company that do a single pass of an LLM to make a decision or provide feedback, but very little real “automation”. Some of this is a statement about the adoption rates of technology in enterprises, but the vast majority of it is really just due to the capability of AI itself.

That’s all changing. Now with computer use, long running agents, harness improvements and surrounding infrastructure, we’re finally at a point where we can start to apply agents at more complex workflows. 

We will see self-improving systems that can take any particular workflow goal and improve the execution rates over a volume of instances. And with the emerging form factor of agent swarms, you can just choose to deploy any amount of compute at a problem and agents will off and do the work.

This won’t be about and users prompting agents to complete a specific task for them, but instead the organization reengineering the underlying workflows to take advantage of agents in their processes. This will have a massive impact in finance, life sciences, healthcare, and other information-heavy domains. Lots of opportunity to build and deploy these systems right now.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
This has been one of the wildest weeks on record for cybersecurity. We've had major disclosures including critical vulnerabilities in PHP, Node.js, and a major certificate authority, forcing governments, major websites, and businesses worldwide to shut down systems to prevent widespread hacking and data theft.

Cyber is going to be one of the most profound aspects of AI. We now have a tireless workforce that can hunt down, discover, patch, or attack any system and software ever created. We will use agents to identify the long standing risks in existing systems and infrastructure.

Attackers will use agents to accelerate the discovery of gaps in environments. We will equally use agents to defend attacks and discover anomalous patterns to better protect our data, and much more.

We’re entering a new cyber regime, and we’ll probably use 100X more tokens on this loop than we’re imagining right now, because we can scan every log, look at every line of code, look through traffic, and process data at a scale that wasn’t comprehensible before.

To prepare for this new reality, more than ever, enterprises are going to care deeply about how they manage their networks, systems, software, identity, devices, and more. And the way we manage our data — how it’s governed, who has access to it, where it’s store, and more — will become especially important in this new era of cyber. 

At Box, we’re incredibly focused on ensuring enterprises have the most advanced capabilities for protecting their unstructured data at scale. As more agents, people, and apps are working on this sensitive information, enterprises will need more capable solutions for preventing threats, detecting issues, locking down data, ensuring only the right people and agents have access to it, classifying data with AI, and more. This is what we’re building at Box. Stay tuned for more.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
This is one of the better litmus tests for whether you’re pushing your use of AI enough or not. 

Up until maybe six months ago probably the best you could do with AI was pull off something you already would produce, but just doing it a little faster. But now we’re entering a point where the output of working with AI can and should dramatically exceed what you would been able to do before, in a fraction of the time.

The product prototype should not only be fully functional and interactive, but it should probably have meaningfully better features than it would have had before. The engineering architecture should be able to deliver performance gains that you wouldn’t have been able to go after otherwise. 

The research for a project should consume every single fact on the subject across every dimension of analysis possible. The business process you implement with AI should operate entirely differently and learn from all its past failures in a way no human could. 

We’re unquestionably entering a period where AI will be smarter than us on most axes. Perhaps not on every dimension that matters (intelligence is still very jagged), but at least on enough dimensions that when we combine it with what we’re good at, you get qualitatively different outcomes.

So the simple test is: if you could have done what you’re doing before AI, you’re likely not pushing it enough.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
Moving from chatting back and forth with agents, to having agents that you spin up in the background to do useful work for you is probably on the order of 100X or 1000X more token consumption than what we’re seeing today. 

Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. 

So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context.

But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”. 

Now imagine that agent swarm for any problem we can think of. Protecting our codebases, data, and systems. QAing every change we make and make sure all our infrastructure is robust and does what it should. Looking through every document for potential risks. Auditing this company with vastly more data reviewed. And on and on. Most of this isn’t even replacing existing work we do, it’s all net new. 

These agents will get deployed as swarms by people, by workflows, by triggers, and by other agents. And none of this would be possible if the models weren’t getting better, and if the cost of AI didn’t make it affordable. Both of those trends though are playing out. Now the next frontier is just having enough compute. But this is where it’s heading.

posts.author: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
Gemini 4 Argon is now out! At Box, we've been testing Gemini 4 Argon on our Box AI Complex Work eval for the past week. It's a huge upgrade over Gemini 3.1 Pro, jumping by 14 percentage points across all our tests, and firmly at the frontier.   

In our evaluation, we give the Box Agent (using Gemini 4 Argon) a variety of complex enterprise tasks involving enterprise documents in a range of industries. These tasks approximate the kind of hard, time-consuming work that knowledge workers do every day with their enterprise content. Gemini 4 is a huge leap on effectively every dimension of this work.  

Gemini 4 is far more capable on math, logic, analytics, and deep knowledge of a variety of business domains. It also works far harder to complete tasks fully without stopping short of the desired result. This is incredibly important for complex enterprise workflows that depend on robust task execution.  

Here are some example wins that we saw to put the improvements in perspective:  

* Financial services (+18 points): a funding-gap analysis for a family-owned company, where the brief spelled out every step of the projected statements, down to the interest on the bank loan and the overdraft for each year. Gemini 4 Argon built them exactly as specified, every line broken out and carried through to the funding gap. Gemini 3.1 Pro folded the interest into a single figure.  

* Healthcare (+25 points): an intensive care management plan where both models spotted a dangerous potassium level and a drug interaction. Only Gemini 4 Argon went back and pulled the offending drugs from the final regimen, so its plan actually matched its own diagnosis.  

* Technology (+37 points): a product performance review deciding which of two regional markets should have its cloud infrastructure optimized first. Gemini 4 Argon pulled the right month's user, retention and per-user figures for both regions and correctly flagged North America. Gemini 3.1 Pro often pulled the wrong rows, at one point reporting retention above 100%, and pointed the effort at the wrong region.  

* Energy (+16 points): an energy consumption report across two facilities that had to flag any gaps in the meter data. Gemini 4 Argon consistently caught that the data center's smart meter log stops in November. Gemini 3.1 Pro often missed it, at times declaring the logs complete.  

* Consumer products (+33 points): a product launch evaluation deciding which production expansion to fund. Gemini 4 Argon saw that existing inventory could bridge an early capacity gap, which made the smaller expansion viable with an earlier launch and a faster break-even. Gemini 3.1 Pro defaulted to the larger expansion and the later timeline.  

Gemini 4 Argon will be available in the Box AI Studio shortly for anyone to build custom Box Agents with. You can learn more here: https://lnkd.in/gAHm6-ac
